newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Ortega offer to meet Aleman eases Nicaragua tension.
newsitem.headline: Ortega offer to meet Aleman eases Nicaragua tension.

text.p: Leftist Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega eased fears of social unrest in Nicaragua on Saturday by accepting an offer for political talks with newly inaugurated President Arnoldo Aleman.

"We are completely disposed to have a dialogue (with Aleman's right-wing Liberal Alliance) ... a dialogue so that we can have a little bit of stability in this country," Ortega, a former president of Nicaragua, told reporters.
Ortega said he would send a letter to Aleman on Saturday asking for a meeting "as soon as possible" and called for the international community's participation in the dialogue.
In his inauguration speech on Friday, Aleman extended an olive branch to Ortega, offering to forget past differences and sit down and talk with his longtime nemesis.

Aleman defeated Ortega in Oct. 20 elections, denying the Sandinistas a chance to regain power after ruling from 1979-90 with Soviet and Cuban support. At the time the Sandinistas faced an insurrection from U.S.-armed Contra rebels.

Even though its civil war ended seven years ago, Nicaragua remains bitterly polarised between the Liberals and Sandinistas, the country's two major political forces, sparking fears of instability and violence.
Analysts say Aleman must reach an agreement with the Sandinistas if he wants to be able to govern effectively.

Aleman took power amid the growing threat of social unrest from the left as Sandinista leaders, angered by what they saw as Liberal efforts to dominate the government, parliament and judiciary, warned of a looming Liberal dictatorship that would force Sandinista activists to take to the streets.
Sandinista leaders still do not recognise the legitimacy of Aleman's government, alleging he won the elections fraudulently.

Aleman's nightmare appeared to be becoming reality on Friday when police arrested two men, both with links to the Sandinista party, carrying four sticks of dynamite and a detonator outside Liberal Alliance party headquarters.

Ortega said the two men, one a retired army officer and the other a former police officer, denied they intended to commit a terrorist act. Ortega said he would wait until more was known before commenting.

On Thursday, the Sandinistas stormed out of parliament's inaugural session to protest a pro-Liberal Supreme Electoral Council decision on vote-taking in parliament. Sandinistas claimed the ruling undermined the rule of law in Nicaragua.

Ortega said the Sandinistas' agenda for talks with Aleman would be the strengthening of the rule of law, the independence of parliament and the judiciary from Liberal control, and Nicaragua's lingering problems over private property.
